source.title: Towards Understanding Grokking: An Effective Theory of Representation Learning
source.authors: Zi-Ming Liu; Ouail Kitouni; Niklas Nolte; Eric J. Michaud; Max Tegmark; Mike Williams

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests delayed generalization on algorithmic tasks and other settings, but uses its own toy model, representation measures, and experiments rather than reproducing the original study’s full method.
record.gate_note: The paper also cites findings from other work; cited findings are not recorded as rows. Rows below use this paper’s own experiments and stated results.
record.test_reason: Own experiments on modular-addition transformers, toy addition/S3 models and MNIST show delayed generalization, its dependence on data size, and how hyperparameters switch it on or off. This is a different method (effective theory, RQI, phase diagrams) aimed at the original question. The study is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that generalization comes from structured representations whose dynamics and critical data-fraction dependence their effective theory predicts in a toy setting. Grokking is one of four phases, lying in a Goldilocks zone with comprehension. In transformers the grokking phase sits close to memorization, and grokking can be removed by tuning decoder capacity and learning speed (weight decay, dropout). The extension to the original transformer setting is called preliminary evidence, and grokking is also induced on MNIST.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses an effective theory and a simplified addition model, adds a modular-addition transformer experiment, and extends the phenomenon to MNIST; it does not reproduce the full original experimental recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with training-data fraction, representation and decoder learning rates, decoder weight decay, dropout, initialization scale, last-layer learning rate, and dataset/training setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Embeddings at initialization, projected onto the final principal axes, already partly contain the generalizing structure (Appendix K, Fig. 21-22).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalizing structure partly exists at initialization and is uncovered by pruning dimensions (lottery-ticket-style).

fits_no_version.finding: The effective loss, applied to MNIST embeddings, collapses same-class representations without contrastive pairs (Appendix I).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The grokking effective theory yields a non-contrastive self-supervised loss and relates to neural collapse.

record.problems: Some key results are presented as phase diagrams or plotted trajectories without exact per-condition values in the text. The paper describes the MNIST grokking setup as nonstandard, using 1000 training samples, large initialization, and MSE with one-hot targets. The effective theory is explicitly a simplified account and the authors note quantitative differences from neural-network training.

untested.parts: Fourier circuit formation; removal of memorizing components; whether continuous measures precede the test-accuracy jump.
Text or molecule data; an explicit lazy-to-rich transition (cited, not measured).
Circuit efficiency or norm comparison of the memorizing vs generalizing solution; ungrokking below critical size.

missing.what: Transformer phase diagram over decoder weight decay and learning rate: weight decay speeds generalization, unlike in the toy
Toy initialization-scale phase diagram: small initialization gives comprehension, large gives memorization
Batch-size phase diagram: small batch with small decoder learning rate gives grokking, large batch gives comprehension
Phase diagrams for addition regression, addition classification and S3 regression: grokking sandwiched between comprehension and memorization
Accuracy predicted from RQI matches empirical accuracy across data fractions

record.verdict_notes: Toy grokking time is defined as steps to RQI>0.95 rather than test-accuracy delay. MNIST grokking required nonstandard choices (1k samples, initialization ×9, MSE loss). The effective-theory rows are predictions, not measurements. Dropout and weight decay act only on the decoder, not the embeddings.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests delayed generalization and training-data-size dependence on algorithmic tasks, but does not test every algorithmic dataset or establish a universal relation across architectures.
It measures embedding structure, RQI, and effective dimension, but does not test a Fourier circuit specifically or directly track memorizing components being removed.
It reports MNIST and hyperparameter effects, including initialization scale, weight decay, and dropout. It does not directly test a lazy-to-rich transition.
No realistic large-model pretraining or fine-tuning experiment.

It tests weight-decay and data-size effects, but does not directly establish that low norm selects a more efficient circuit, measure circuit efficiency, or test ungrokking below a critical dataset size.
No test of whether runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm.
No test of adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point/softmax artifacts.

rows.subject: decoder-only transformer (p = 53)
rows.operation_detail: Train on modular addition and report train and validation accuracy at the overfitting stage.
rows.note: The paper identifies this point as overfitting.
rows.check: Fine. Train acc 1.0 vs val acc 0.1 at 1000 iterations (Fig. 1).

rows.subject: decoder-only transformer (p = 53)
rows.operation_detail: Continue training on modular addition and report train and validation accuracy alongside embedding structure.
rows.measure: training and validation accuracy; embedding structure in PCA
rows.baseline: r1: train acc 1.0 and val acc 0.1 at 1000 iterations
rows.value: train acc: 1.0; val acc: 1.0; paper reports structure emerging in the embeddings
rows.note: The paper says perfect generalization coincides with the PCA projection of the embeddings forming a circle.
rows.check: Observed for V1. For V2 the authors say PCA/t-SNE show no structure before generalization; structure appears coinciding with it, not ahead of it. The V2 state is cannot_determine, because the authors note PCA may miss structure.

source_check.correct: V1: observed when compared with r1. V2: cannot_determine; the snapshots show structure coinciding with generalization, without measuring gradual circuit formation or earlier removal of memorization.
source_check.locator_found: Figure 1; Section 4.2, paragraphs discussing PCA and t-SNE.
source_check.problem: The shared observed state overstates what the snapshots establish for V2.

rows.subject: toy neural network, addition (p = 10)
rows.operation_detail: Measure empirical representation quality (RQI) across training-data fractions.
rows.measure: RQI / probability of obtaining linear structure
rows.value: empirical RQI has a phase transition around rc = 0.4
rows.uncertainty: blue line is the median of multiple random seeds
rows.note: The text says empirical results display a phase transition of RQI around rc = 0.4.
rows.check: Fig. 4b plots steps to RQI>0.95 against data fraction, a critical-size/timing result, not a V2 progress-measure result. Relinked from V2 to V1/V5.

source_check.correct: Figure 4(b) measures steps to RQI > 0.95, with a transition around training fraction 0.4; its blue line is the median across seeds. The probability of obtaining a linear representation belongs to theoretical Figure 4(a). V1: cannot_determine the full accuracy-delay claim from this representation-timing measure. V5: threshold component only.
source_check.problem: The measure conflates theoretical probability with empirical representation timing, which does not establish the full V1 accuracy trajectory.

rows.subject: toy neural network, addition (p = 10)
rows.operation_detail: Compare the learned representation trajectory with the effective-theory trajectory.
rows.value: the two trajectories agree qualitatively; convergence to the linear structure takes about 3nh steps
rows.note: The paper notes quantitative differences and attributes them possibly to the decoder being absent from the effective theory.
rows.check: Compares theory and NN embedding trajectories in a toy without a delayed accuracy jump. It cannot show whether a progress measure anticipates grokking.

rows.subject: effective theory for toy addition (p = 10)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate the theoretical grokking rate as training-data fraction varies.
rows.value: below a threshold around 0.4, λ3 is zero with high probability; above the threshold, λ3 on average increases with data size
rows.uncertainty: λ3 is described as a probabilistic function of data size because many datasets have the same size
rows.note: The paper interprets zero rate as corresponding to no generalization and increasing rate as implying shorter grokking time.
rows.check: This is the authors' theoretical prediction (λ3 from the effective loss), not a neural-network measurement. V2 link removed. The critical size comes from data constraints with no weight-decay term.

source_check.correct: The effective theory predicts λ3 = 0 with high probability below approximately 0.4 and increasing average λ3 above it. V1: cannot_determine the full empirical accuracy-delay claim. V5: theoretical threshold prediction only; low-norm circuit selection and ungrokking are not demonstrated.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, dependence of grokking on data size; Figure 5(a).
source_check.problem: A theoretical representation-rate prediction is recorded as an observed instance of the full V1 behavior.

rows.subject: toy neural network, addition (p = 10)
rows.operation_detail: Compare empirical steps to RQI > 0.95 across training-data fractions with effective-theory predictions.
rows.value: theory and neural-network results agree qualitatively, showing decreasing grokking steps as data size increases
rows.note: The paper defines empirical grokking steps here by reaching RQI > 0.95.
rows.check: Grokking time is measured as steps to RQI>0.95, not test-accuracy delay. V2 link removed.

source_check.correct: The predicted number of steps scales as 1/(λ3η), with η = 10^-3. Empirical steps to RQI > 0.95 decrease with increasing training fraction and agree qualitatively with theory. V1: cannot_determine the full test-accuracy-delay claim from this timing proxy.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, equations following the Hessian definition and subsequent comparison; Figure 5(b) caption.
source_check.problem: The baseline places η outside the reciprocal; the observed state also conflates representation timing with the full V1 accuracy trajectory.

rows.subject: toy model, addition group
rows.operation_detail: Sweep decoder and representation learning rates and decoder weight decay; classify learning phases by accuracy and timing thresholds.
rows.measure: learning phase, based on training/validation accuracy and delay
rows.value: comprehension, grokking, memorization, and confusion phases occur; a fast decoder with slow representation learning leads to memorization, while the opposite extreme generalizes only after a long time
rows.note: The paper defines high accuracy using 90% thresholds within 10^5 steps, with grokking distinguished from comprehension by a validation-versus-training timing difference.
rows.check: Main bearing: grokking is one of four phases. The comprehension phase generalizes without delay on the same data, so the delay depends on learning rates and decoder weight decay. Large decoder weight decay gives confusion, not comprehension.

source_check.correct: Use condition-specific states: V1 observed in the grokking phase and absent in comprehension, memorization and confusion. The sweep establishes training-regime dependence, but does not directly measure V5 circuit efficiency. Table 1 uses >90% training/validation accuracy within 10^5 steps and a 10^3-step delay boundary.
source_check.problem: One observed state hides different outcomes across the swept conditions and overstates direct evidence for the efficiency mechanism.

rows.subject: transformer, modular addition (p = 53)
rows.operation_detail: Vary dropout in decoder blocks to constrain the decoder.

conditions.value: significant rate; exact value not stated

rows.value: generalization time can be brought down to under 10^3 steps and the grokking phenomenon vanishes completely
rows.note: The paper states that constraining the decoder reduces generalization time and can avoid grokking.
rows.check: The knob is dropout, not initialization or weight norm. It shows grokking can be removed on the algorithmic task. V5 link removed.

source_check.correct: V1: absent under significant decoder dropout; generalization occurs in under 10^3 steps and the delay disappears. This row supports the training-regime component of V3 on an algorithmic task; it does not itself establish non-algorithmic grokking or a lazy-to-rich transition.
source_check.problem: Observed is incorrect for V1 in a condition explicitly reported to eliminate grokking.

rows.subject: transformer, modular addition (p = 53)
rows.operation_detail: Track entropy of explained variance in embedding PCA during training.
rows.measure: effective dimension / entropy of PCA explained variance
rows.value: entropy increases up to generalization time, then decreases drastically
rows.note: The authors say this pattern is consistent with a low-dimensional structure being discovered.
rows.check: Entropy rises until generalization and then drops sharply. The measure turns at the jump rather than clearly anticipating it, and it does not isolate memorizing components.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, PCA explained-variance entropy discussion; Figure 7 left.

rows.subject: depth-3 width-200 MLP with ReLU activations
rows.operation_detail: Train on MNIST with increased initialization scale and reduced training set.
rows.measure: training and validation accuracy over training
rows.value: the network quickly fits the training set, and much later validation accuracy improves
rows.note: The paper describes this as closely following the stereotypical grokking learning pattern.

rows.subject: depth-3 width-200 MLP with ReLU activations
rows.operation_detail: Vary MNIST training-set size and measure time to validation accuracy above 60%.
rows.value: generalization time increases rapidly once training size drops below a certain amount
rows.uncertainty: figure marks runs that did and did not reach 60% validation accuracy in 10^5 steps; exact values not stated
rows.note: The text states the trend is similar to the data-size result reported by Power et al.

source_check.correct: Observed: rapid growth in steps to validation accuracy >60% as MNIST training size decreases, at weight decay 5e-3. V3: cannot_determine delayed generalization or switching through initialization/norm from this scaling row alone; those require Figure 8 and the other Appendix J experiments.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix J; Figure 20, including its axis labels and run-status legend.
source_check.problem: The row measures data-size dependence of validation timing, not the train–validation delay or regime switch named by V3.

rows.subject: depth-3 width-200 MLP with ReLU activations
rows.operation_detail: Sweep model weight decay and last-layer learning rate on MNIST.
rows.measure: learning phase from training and validation accuracy timing
rows.value: the phase diagram contains confusion, comprehension, grokking, and memorization regions; sufficient regularization can de-grok learning
rows.note: The authors treat the last layer as the decoder for this phase diagram.

rows.subject: toy model, permutation group S3
rows.operation_detail: Vary training-data fraction and measure RQI and steps to RQI > 0.95.
rows.value: RQI increases as training set becomes larger; steps to RQI > 0.95 show a phase transition around rc = 0.5
rows.uncertainty: 11 random seeds per training-data fraction; plotted blue line is the highest RQI or the smallest number of steps, respectively
rows.note: These are representation and timing results for a non-Abelian algorithmic task.
rows.check: Timing is steps to RQI>0.95, best seed of 11. V2 link removed.

source_check.correct: The S3 experiment uses 11 seeds per training fraction. Figure 18(a) reports the highest RQI and Figure 18(b) the smallest number of steps to RQI >0.95, with a transition around 0.5. V1: cannot_determine its full accuracy-delay trajectory from these representation measures. V5: threshold component only.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix H.2, RQI and timing paragraphs; Figure 18(a–b) caption.
source_check.problem: Representation quality and best-seed representation timing do not establish the full V1 accuracy-delay claim.

relationships.condition: transformer on modular addition (p=53); toy addition and S3 data-fraction sweeps
relationships.reason: Train acc 1.0/val 0.1 at 1k steps, both 1.0 at 20k (r1, r2). No generalization below rc≈0.4 (addition) or 0.5 (S3), and grokking steps fall as data grows (r3, r5, r6, r13).
relationships.display_finding: Training and validation accuracy were 1.0 and 0.1 at 1,000 steps and both 1.0 at 20,000 steps; generalization failed below training fractions of approximately 0.4 for addition and 0.5 for S3, while larger fractions shortened grokking.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: transformer on modular addition (p=53); toy addition and S3 data-fraction sweeps
source_check.reason: r1–r2 establish delayed transformer generalization. The toy sweeps provide supporting data-size dependence through representation-timing proxies, rather than direct measurements of the complete accuracy trajectory.

relationships.condition: hyperparameter choice (decoder/representation learning rate, weight decay, dropout)
relationships.reason: Delay is not intrinsic to the data. A comprehension phase generalizes without delay, and significant dropout brings generalization under 10^3 steps with grokking vanishing (r7, r8).
relationships.display_finding: The comprehension phase generalized without delay, and substantial dropout brought generalization below 1,000 steps while eliminating grokking.

relationships.condition: embedding PCA and effective-dimension measures in the modular-addition transformer
relationships.reason: No visible structure before generalization; the structure and the entropy drop coincide with the jump rather than precede it (r2, r9).

source_check.condition: embedding PCA and effective-dimension measures in the modular-addition transformer

relationships.condition: MNIST MLP with 1k training points and initialization scale 9; hyperparameter phase diagrams
relationships.reason: MNIST shows fast train fit with much later validation gain (r10). Generalization time rises sharply at small train size (r11). Weight decay and learning-rate settings switch grokking on or off on MNIST and toy tasks (r7, r12).
relationships.display_finding: Validation improved long after training fit, with sharply longer delays at smaller training sizes and grokking appearing or disappearing across weight-decay and learning-rate settings.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: MNIST MLP with 1k training points and initialization scale 9; hyperparameter phase diagrams
source_check.reason: Figure 8 and Appendix J show delayed MNIST generalization with 1000 points and initialization scale 9, and phase changes with weight decay and last-layer learning rate. A lazy-to-rich mechanism is discussed rather than directly established.

relationships.condition: critical data size in toy addition, S3 and MNIST
relationships.reason: A critical training fraction exists, below which generalization fails or slows sharply (r3, r5, r11, r13). Decoder weight decay speeds transformer generalization (Fig. 7 right, from text; not in rows).
relationships.display_finding: Generalization failed or slowed sharply below a critical training fraction, while decoder weight decay accelerated transformer generalization.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: critical data size in toy addition, S3 and MNIST
source_check.reason: The results support the threshold/data-size prediction component: approximately 0.4 in toy addition, approximately 0.5 in S3 representation timing, and rapid MNIST slowing at small training sizes. They do not establish the efficiency mechanism or ungrokking.

relationships.condition: toy effective theory and toy decoder weight-decay sweeps
relationships.reason: The critical size is derived from parallelogram constraints in the data with no low-norm bias (r5). In the toy, large decoder weight decay leads to confusion rather than better generalization (r7).
relationships.display_finding: Parallelogram constraints yielded a critical data size without low-norm bias, while excessive decoder weight decay caused confusion rather than improved generalization.

relation.reason: The study reports its own transformer, toy-model and MNIST experiments bearing on delayed generalization and its conditions.

tranche.reason: The effective theory, representation-quality measurements and phase diagrams use a different method to investigate the origin, data-size dependence and training-regime dependence of grokking.

source_check.notes: RQI timing is a representation-based proxy, and the S3 timing curve selects the best of 11 seeds. Threshold evidence and decoder-decay benefits should be distinguished from direct evidence for circuit efficiency or ungrokking.

statements.correction: Modulus 53 transformer; significant decoder dropout; generalization under 10^3 steps; grokking disappears; V1 limits_scope for this training condition.
statements.problem: The dropout result and modular-addition setting are correct, but challenges overstates this study's condition-specific evidence under the verdict rules.

statements.correction: Toy threshold derived from parallelogram constraints; effective dynamics conserve embedding squared norm; excessive decoder decay can produce confusion; circuit-efficiency selection and ungrokking untested.
statements.problem: The theoretical threshold and confusion phase are accurately described, but they do not directly test or delimit selection of an efficient circuit by low-norm bias.
